newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FCC adopts rule on long-distance rates.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FCC adopts rule on long-distance rates.

text.p: The Federal Communications Commission eliminated a Depression-era rule Tuesday requiring U.S. long distance phone companies to notify the agency beforehand of rate changes.

The new rule, adopted at a public meeting, is designed to instill more competition into the $70 billion long-distance market and reduce government red tape for AT&T Corp and other long-distance phone companies.
The old rule, that dates to the 1930s, required long-distance companies to tell the FCC in advance of plans to change rates or offer new services through "tariff" filings.

The FCC said that long-distance companies will still be required to disclose publicly information about their rates and services. Some carriers are expected to unveil their rates, for example, over the Internet.

The new approach is the first major step the FCC has taken under a key provision of the new telecommunications law allowing the agency to shed rules it considers outdated as long as the public interest is unharmed.
FCC officials said the rise of competition in the long-distance phone market made the tariff filings no longer necessary.

The 1934 rule was intended originally to allow regulators to review rate changes while giving the public an advance look, although the language in the filings often was arcane and read by few persons.

Industry officials had sought -- but without success -- to retain the option of filing tariffs for certain residential telephone plans saying that would make it easier to let consumers know what their phone rates are.

The new approach is expected to reduce paperwork at the FCC. In fiscal year 1996 companies submitted more than 4,200 tariff filings with the agency. They amounted to more than 250,000 pieces of paper.
